disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, with no history of full manic episodes. Hypomanic episodes involve a sustained period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased activity or energy that is observable by others but not severe enough to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. Depressive episodes tend to be prominent and often drive help‑seeking, with significant impact on functioning and quality of life. Compared with Bipolar I Disorder, Bipolar II often presents with less dramatic mood elevation but more chronic or recurrent depression, and it can be misdiagnosed as unipolar depression if hypomanic periods are not carefully elicited.

narrative.personality: A quietly driven, detail‑oriented problem solver, Alex channels solitary, art‑focused curiosity into meticulous work and creative side projects, often pushing himself past reasonable limits.
narrative.stressor: Over the past several months, Alex has been working in a high‑volume call center that recently shifted to more aggressive performance metrics and mandatory overtime during a major product rollout. Wanting to prove himself for a potential team‑lead promotion, he began volunteering for extra shifts while simultaneously pouring energy into a homebrewing project and an online portfolio of his design sketches, leaving little time for rest or social connection outside his marriage. Initially he felt unusually energized and productive, staying up late to redesign ticket dashboards and obsessively refine his creative work, but as the weeks went on this constant push eroded his routine, led to mounting exhaustion, and made it harder to sustain his usual methodical self‑care habits. When his performance at work became inconsistent, his wife noticed his growing withdrawal and urged him to see a psychiatrist after he started complaining that he felt completely drained despite cutting back on some of his commitments.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel exhausted all the time, like I never have any energy even when I try to rest.

narrative.personality: Janice is a competitive, data‑driven retail leader with a strong creative streak, who thrives on visual projects and late‑night brainstorming but tends to run herself hard when chasing new goals.
narrative.stressor: In the past year, Janice finalized a difficult divorce while simultaneously taking on expanded responsibilities at her store as she positioned herself for a regional district‑manager role. With her evenings now largely her own, she began filling the time with ambitious merchandising plans, late‑night pottery and painting sessions, and extensive strategic planning for her career, telling herself that staying busy helped her avoid dwelling on the divorce. During a recent seasonal reset, she rode a wave of intense drive and creativity, sleeping only a few hours a night yet still showing up early to reorganize displays and coach her team, convinced she was finally hitting her stride. After several weeks of this pace, colleagues commented on how "wired" she seemed, and when she found she could no longer wind down enough to sleep more than a couple of hours despite feeling physically worn, she agreed to consult a psychiatrist at the suggestion of her primary care provider, who was concerned about the abrupt and sustained change in her sleep and energy patterns.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I only sleep a few hours a night and still feel wired, like I just can’t shut my mind off.

narrative.personality: Lucas is a highly organized, analytical planner who enjoys structured problem‑solving and technical hobbies, but can become overly absorbed in projects and neglect basic routines.
narrative.stressor: Several months ago, Lucas was assigned as the lead systems analyst on a high‑stakes enterprise migration project with tight deadlines and significant visibility to senior management. Determined to anticipate every possible complication, he immersed himself in the work, extending his usual meticulous planning into long evenings of documentation, testing scenarios, and tinkering with related DIY electronics projects at home. He noticed that during one particularly intense month he felt unusually driven and focused, staying up until the early morning hours working on architecture diagrams or coding small tools, yet still arriving at the office early and insisting he felt fine despite barely sleeping. When the project entered a quieter phase, his concentration and mood dipped, and he became concerned by how abruptly his energy and sleep patterns had shifted over that month; after a colleague mentioned their own experience with mood disorders and suggested an evaluation, he sought psychiatric consultation to understand why his sleep had changed so dramatically during that period.
narrative.chief_complaint: For about a month I was only sleeping around three hours a night but still felt like I didn’t need any more rest.
